title: The Byzantine Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Byzantine Empire, the eastern Roman Empire ruled from Constantinople, from Constantine’s new capital through Justinian and the Hagia Sophia, the plague, Heraclius and the Arab conquests, Greek fire, the icons, Basil II, Manzikert, the Fourth Crusade and Mistra to the fall of the city in 1453.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Byzantine Empire, 330 to 1453
note: Based mainly on Byzantine historians and chroniclers (Procopius, Theophanes, Michael Psellos, John Skylitzes, Niketas Choniates and George Sphrantzes), on Arab and Western accounts, and on the modern record; each chapter says which it follows. Their numbers for armies and deaths are often too large and are given as theirs. Native names are given in Latin letters. The map is stylised and not to scale. Italy and North Africa, which Justinian won back, lie beyond the map’s western edge. Coasts are drawn as they are today. Lands under Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: New Rome on the Bosporus
steps.text: The emperor Constantine refounds the old Greek town of Byzantium as his new capital and dedicates it on 11 May 330. Standing where Europe meets Asia, it guards the Bosporus and the roads to the eastern frontier. Its people call themselves Romans (Rhomaioi), and Constantine favours Christianity. Only centuries later did historians call this eastern empire “Byzantine”.
steps.today: Today: Istanbul, Turkey; its historic peninsula is a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Justinian and the Hagia Sophia
steps.text: Justinian I survives the Nika riot of 532, when crowds burn much of the city, and rebuilds the church of Hagia Sophia (Holy Wisdom) under a vast dome, finished in 537. His lawyers gather centuries of Roman law into one code. His generals, chief among them Belisarius, retake North Africa and Italy, but the long wars exhaust the empire.
steps.today: Today: the Hagia Sophia still stands in Istanbul, a mosque again since 2020.

steps.title: The plague arrives
steps.text: Plague breaks out at Pelusium, a port on the eastern edge of the Nile delta, in 541 and spreads along the shipping routes to Constantinople by spring 542. The historian Procopius describes thousands dying each day; modern estimates of the toll vary widely and are disputed. Ancient DNA from graves shows the cause was the bubonic plague bacterium (Yersinia pestis).
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Tell el-Farama, east of Port Said, Egypt.

steps.title: Heraclius strikes back
steps.text: In a long war the Persian king Khosrow II takes Syria, Jerusalem and Egypt, and in 626 Persians and Avars besiege Constantinople together. The emperor Heraclius strikes deep into Persia instead and wins a battle near the ruins of Nineveh in December 627. Khosrow is overthrown, and in 630 Heraclius returns the True Cross to Jerusalem.
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Nineveh lie within the city of Mosul, Iraq.

steps.title: The Arabs take Syria
steps.text: Only six years after Heraclius’s triumph, Arab Muslim armies sent by the caliph from Medina break the Roman army beside the Yarmouk river. Syria and Jerusalem are lost, and Egypt follows by 642. The empire loses its richest provinces and most of its grain, and shrinks to Anatolia, the Aegean, Constantinople and parts of the Balkans and Italy.
steps.today: Today: the Yarmouk valley, on the border between Jordan and Syria.

steps.title: Greek fire and the great siege
steps.text: An Umayyad army and fleet besiege Constantinople for a year. The emperor Leo III holds the walls, ships armed with Greek fire, a liquid that burned even on water, destroy much of the Arab fleet, and Bulgar allies attack the besiegers. Cold and hunger do the rest, and the siege ends in August 718. Greek fire’s recipe is still unknown.
steps.today: Today: long stretches of the land walls still stand along Istanbul’s western edge.

steps.title: The icons restored
steps.text: From about the 720s, emperors attack holy images (icons) as idolatry, and many are destroyed; this is called Iconoclasm. In 787 the empress Irene calls a church council at Nicaea, where Constantine had held the first great council in 325, and it restores the icons. A second wave of Iconoclasm follows, ending for good in 843.
steps.today: Today: the town of İznik, Turkey, where the council’s church, also called Hagia Sophia, survives as a mosque.

steps.title: The Bulgar-slayer
steps.text: Basil II spends decades at war with Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria. In 1014 his troops outflank Samuel’s army at the Kleidion pass. The chronicler Skylitzes says Basil blinded about 15,000 prisoners, leaving one eye to every hundredth man to lead them home; the number is disputed. Samuel dies soon after, and by 1018 Bulgaria is conquered.
steps.today: Today: the Belasitsa mountains, near where Bulgaria, Greece and North Macedonia meet.

steps.title: Defeat at Manzikert
steps.text: The emperor Romanos IV Diogenes marches east against the Seljuk Turks and meets Sultan Alp Arslan near Manzikert. Part of his army deserts or holds back, and Romanos is captured. The sultan frees him on terms, but civil war follows in Constantinople, and within a few years Turkish groups settle across Anatolia, the empire’s heartland of soldiers and taxes.
steps.today: Today: the town of Malazgirt, in eastern Turkey, north of Lake Van.

steps.title: The Fourth Crusade
steps.text: A crusade bound for Egypt, in debt to Venice for its fleet, is drawn into a quarrel over the Byzantine throne and turns on Constantinople. On 13 April 1204 the crusaders storm the city and sack it for three days, taking relics and treasure, including the bronze horses now in Venice. They crown a Latin emperor, Baldwin of Flanders.
steps.today: Today: the four bronze horses taken in 1204 are in St Mark’s Basilica, Venice.

steps.title: An empire in exile
steps.text: Byzantine nobles set up rival states at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond. Nicaea, under Theodore I Laskaris and then John III Vatatzes, grows strongest. On 25 July 1261 a small force sent by Michael VIII Palaiologos slips into Constantinople while most of the Latin garrison is away, and the city is Roman again. The restored empire is smaller and poorer.
steps.today: Today: İznik, Turkey; its Roman and Byzantine walls and gates still ring the town.

steps.title: The last flowering
steps.text: By the 1400s the empire is little more than Constantinople, a few islands and the Morea in southern Greece, ruled from the hill town of Mistra. Here the scholar George Gemistos Plethon teaches Plato, and Greek learning travels on to Italy. In 1449 the despot of the Morea is proclaimed emperor at Mistra and sails to Constantinople as Constantine XI.
steps.today: Today: the ruins of Mystras, near Sparti, Greece; a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: The fall of the city
steps.text: Sultan Mehmed II marches from Edirne with a large army, its size disputed. Huge cannon batter the land walls for seven weeks, while Constantine XI defends them with fewer than 8,000 men. On 29 May the Ottomans break in, and the last emperor dies fighting. The city becomes the Ottoman capital, and the Hagia Sophia a mosque.
steps.today: Today: Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city; the Hagia Sophia is again a mosque.

items.name: Latin Empire
items.role: The crusaders’ state at Constantinople, with Venice holding many ports and islands.

items.name: Ottoman Empire
items.role: The Turkish state founded by Osman in northwest Anatolia, which surrounded Constantinople.

items.name: Constantine the Great
items.text: Constantine fought his way to sole rule of the Roman Empire by 324. He was the first emperor to back Christianity, ending its persecution, and he called the church council at Nicaea in 325. He refounded Byzantium as Constantinople, his new capital, in 330. He was baptised only on his deathbed in 337.

items.name: Justinian I
items.text: A farmer’s nephew from the Balkans who rose to the throne. He ordered the great law code later called the Body of Civil Law (Corpus Juris Civilis), the base of civil law in much of Europe, built the Hagia Sophia and won back Italy and North Africa. Procopius says he caught the plague in 542 and survived.

items.name: Theodora
items.text: Procopius says she had been an actress, a lowly trade, before marrying Justinian. During the Nika riot, he reports, she urged Justinian to stay and fight rather than flee, saying royalty makes a fine burial shroud. She shaped his policies, protected Miaphysite Christians and backed laws for women. Her portrait in mosaic survives at Ravenna.

items.name: Heraclius
items.text: Son of the governor of Africa, he sailed from Carthage and overthrew the emperor Phocas in 610. He won the long war against Persia and brought the True Cross back to Jerusalem, then lost Syria and Egypt to the Arab armies within a few years. In his reign Greek replaced Latin as the language of government.

items.name: Irene
items.text: Regent for her young son Constantine VI, she called the council that restored the icons in 787. In 797 she had her son blinded and ruled alone, the first woman to rule the empire in her own name. In 800, arguing partly that a woman could not hold the throne, the pope crowned Charlemagne emperor in the West.

items.name: Basil II
items.text: Basil reigned longer than any other Byzantine emperor. He crushed rebel generals with 6,000 Varangian warriors sent by Prince Vladimir of Kyiv, who in return married Basil’s sister Anna and was baptised, bringing the Rus into Orthodox Christianity. He conquered Bulgaria and was later called the Bulgar-slayer (Boulgaroktonos). He never married.

items.name: Constantine XI Palaiologos
items.text: As despot of the Morea he rebuilt the Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus of Corinth. As emperor he accepted union with the Roman Catholic Church, hoping for Western help, which angered many of his people. He refused Mehmed’s offer to surrender the city and died in the final assault; his body was never certainly identified.

items.name: Mehmed II
items.text: He became sultan for good at 19, and in 1452 built the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosporus to cut the city off from the Black Sea. He took Constantinople the next year, aged 21, and was called the Conqueror (Fatih). He brought back an Orthodox patriarch, resettled the city and began the Topkapı Palace.
